title: Regularization III - Elastic Net
abstract:
Elastic Net is the combination of Ridge and Lasso: it adds both penalties at once
and lets you choose the mix. The notes state its purpose precisely — use it when
the dataset is large and you are confused about whether to use $L_1$ or $L_2$, and
because it works well when the input columns have high multicollinearity.
This document works the objective, the two hyperparameters and the two competing
parameterisations, the grouping effect that fixes Lasso's arbitrary choice among
correlated features, why the $L_2$ term removes Lasso's $p>n$ limit, and how to
tune the pair.

blocks.t: The Objective
From the notes

items:
If the dataset is large and you are confused whether to use $L_1$
 or $L_2$ regularization.

blocks.t:
\boxed{ \text{Loss}=\text{Loss}+\underbrace{a\left|w\right|^{2}}_{\text{Ridge}}
 +\underbrace{b\left|w\right|}_{\text{Lasso}} }

items: Works well when the input columns have high multicollinearity.

blocks.t: Written out

L_{\text{enet}}(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i-\hat y_i\right)^{2}
 + a\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2} + b\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left|\beta_j\right|

Setting $b=0$ recovers Ridge; setting $a=0$ recovers Lasso. Elastic Net is the
whole two-dimensional family that contains both as edges.
The Two Parameterisations
The notes use $(a,b)$; scikit-learn uses $(\alpha, \ell_1)$
scikit-learn reparameterises the same objective as
so the translation is

b = \alpha \ell_1 \quad(\text{the }L_1\text{ weight}),
 \qquad
 a = \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha\left(1-\ell_1\right)\quad(\text{the }L_2\text{ weight}).

This factorisation is deliberate and more convenient: alpha
controls the overall strength of regularisation and l1_ratio
controls the mix. The two are close to independent, so a grid search over them
behaves far better than a grid over $(a,b)$ directly.

rows: Pure Ridge — shrink everything, drop nothing

blocks.cap:
The constraint region as l1_ratio varies. It morphs
 continuously from a circle (Ridge, no corners, no sparsity) to a diamond
 (Lasso, sharp corners, aggressive sparsity). Intermediate values have corners
 that are present but blunted — sparsity, applied more gently.

blocks.t: The Grouping Effect
Why it works well under high multicollinearity

This is the property that motivated Elastic Net (Zou & Hastie, 2005) and the one
the notes single out.

Recall Lasso's weakness (Topic 42): given several near-identical predictors it
keeps one, arbitrarily, and which one flips with small changes in the data.
Ridge instead splits the weight evenly among them but never removes any.

Elastic Net does both: the $L_2$ term encourages correlated predictors to receive
similar coefficients, while the $L_1$ term still removes the genuinely
irrelevant ones. Correlated features therefore enter or leave the model
as a group.

blocks.cap:
Left: five near-identical features plus five independent ones. Lasso
 gives almost all the weight to one of the five and zeroes the rest; Ridge
 spreads it evenly but keeps every irrelevant feature too; Elastic Net spreads
 the weight across the group and prunes the irrelevant ones. Right: the
 bootstrap instability of the coefficients rises with l1_ratio, while the
 number of group members retained falls.

blocks.t: The grouping bound

For two standardised predictors with correlation $\rho$, the Elastic Net solution
satisfies

\frac{\left|\hat\beta_i-\hat\beta_j\right|}{\|y\|_1}
 \le \frac{\sqrt{2\left(1-\rho\right)}}{a}

where $a$ is the $L_2$ weight. As $\rho\to1$ the right-hand side tends to zero, so
perfectly correlated predictors are forced to receive identical
coefficients. No such bound exists for Lasso, which is precisely why its choice
among them is arbitrary.
Two More Things the $L_2$ Term Buys

rows: Lasso can select at most $n$ features (Topic 42). Adding any $L_2$ term lifts that limit — Elastic Net can select more predictors than there are rows, which matters in genomics and text
With $a>0$ the objective is strictly convex even when $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular, so the solution is unique. Pure Lasso on collinear data can have a whole set of equally optimal solutions

blocks.t: Choosing the Two Hyperparameters

blocks.cap:
Cross-validated error over the two-dimensional grid. The surface is
 usually shallow along l1_ratio and steep along alpha — so the
 overall strength matters more than the mix, which is exactly why the
 scikit-learn parameterisation is the useful one.

blocks.t: A practical search strategy

Search l1_ratio over a coarse grid weighted towards 1 — the
scikit-learn documentation suggests [.1, .5, .7, .9, .95, .99, 1] — and
alpha over a log-spaced range. ElasticNetCV does this efficiently
using warm starts along the regularisation path, which is far cheaper than a naive
GridSearchCV that refits from scratch at every point.
When to Use Which

head: Method
Use when
Because
rows: All features are important; features are correlated
Shrinks without removing; stabilises collinear coefficients
Many features are irrelevant; you want a sparse model
Drives irrelevant coefficients to exactly zero
The dataset is large and you are unsure which to use; high multicollinearity
Gets selection from $L_1$ and stability from $L_2$; groups correlated features

blocks.t: The honest summary

Elastic Net is the safe default when you do not know the answer, because it
contains both alternatives — cross-validation can select
l1_ratio $=0$ or $1$ if that is genuinely best. The cost is a
two-dimensional search instead of one-dimensional, and slower fitting. When the
structure is clear — all features relevant, or most irrelevant — the
single-penalty method is simpler and just as good.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import (ElasticNet, ElasticNetCV, Lasso, Ridge,
                                  LinearRegression, SGDRegressor)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. A DATASET WITH EXACTLY THE STRUCTURE ELASTIC NET IS FOR
# =====================================================================
n = 200
z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
group  = np.c_[[z + rng.normal(0, .05, n) for _ in range(5)]].T   # 5 near-identical
useful = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 2))                                  # 2 independent, real
noise  = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 13))                                 # 13 irrelevant
X = np.c_[group, useful, noise]
y = 3 * z + useful @ np.array([1.5, -1.0]) + rng.normal(0, .6, n)
print("shape:", X.shape, " (0-4 correlated group, 5-6 useful, 7-19 noise)")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE THREE PENALTIES SIDE BY SIDE
# =====================================================================
models = {
    "OLS":        LinearRegression(),
    "Ridge":      Ridge(alpha=1.0),
    "Lasso":      Lasso(alpha=0.1, max_iter=50000),
    "ElasticNet": ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=50000),
}
print(f"\n{'model':12s} {'group coefs (0-4)':>34s} {'nonzero':>9s} {'cv R2':>8s}")
for name, m in models.items():
    c = m.fit(X, y).coef_
    cv = cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:12s} {np.array2string(c[:5], precision=2, suppress_small=True):>34s} "
          f"{int((c != 0).sum()):9d} {cv:8.4f}")
# Lasso puts ~all the group weight on ONE feature and zeroes the other four.
# Ridge spreads it evenly but keeps all 13 noise features too.
# ElasticNet spreads across the group AND prunes the noise.

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE GROUPING EFFECT, AND ITS STABILITY
# =====================================================================
print("\nrefitting on bootstrap samples -- which group member survives?")
for tag, mdl in [("Lasso     ", Lasso(alpha=.1, max_iter=50000)),
                 ("ElasticNet", ElasticNet(alpha=.1, l1_ratio=.5, max_iter=50000))]:
    for s in range(4):
        idx = np.random.default_rng(s).choice(n, n, replace=True)
        c = mdl.fit(X[idx], y[idx]).coef_[:5]
        print(f"  {tag} sample {s}: {np.array2string(c, precision=2, suppress_small=True)}")
# Lasso's single survivor CHANGES between samples. Elastic Net's spread does not.

# quantify it:
for tag, mdl in [("Lasso", Lasso(alpha=.1, max_iter=50000)),
                 ("ElasticNet", ElasticNet(alpha=.1, l1_ratio=.5, max_iter=50000)),
                 ("Ridge", Ridge(alpha=1.0))]:
    cs = np.array([mdl.fit(X[i], y[i]).coef_[:5]
                   for i in (np.random.default_rng(s).choice(n, n, replace=True)
                             for s in range(50))])
    print(f"{tag:12s} bootstrap sd across the group: {cs.std(0).mean():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. l1_ratio SWEEPS BETWEEN THE TWO EXTREMES
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'l1_ratio':>10s} {'nonzero':>9s} {'group kept':>12s} {'cv R2':>8s}")
for r in [0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0]:
    m = (Ridge(alpha=.1) if r == 0
         else ElasticNet(alpha=.1, l1_ratio=r, max_iter=50000))
    c = m.fit(X, y).coef_
    cv = cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{r:10.2f} {int((c != 0).sum()):9d} {int((c[:5] != 0).sum()):12d} {cv:8.4f}")
# r=0 keeps all 20. r=1 keeps ~1 of the group. Intermediate values keep the
# GROUP together while removing the noise.

# =====================================================================
# 5. TRANSLATING THE NOTES' (a, b) TO SKLEARN'S (alpha, l1_ratio)
# =====================================================================
def to_sklearn(a, b, n_samples):
    """notes:  loss + a*|w|^2 + b*|w|   ->  sklearn (alpha, l1_ratio)."""
    alpha = (b + 2 * a) / n_samples      # sklearn divides the loss by 2n
    l1_ratio = b / (b + 2 * a)
    return alpha, l1_ratio

for a, b in [(1.0, 0.0), (0.0, 1.0), (0.5, 0.5), (0.2, 1.0)]:
    al, r = to_sklearn(a, b, n)
    kind = "pure Ridge" if r == 0 else "pure Lasso" if r == 1 else "mixture"
    print(f"a={a:.1f} b={b:.1f}  ->  alpha={al:.5f} l1_ratio={r:.3f}   ({kind})")
# a controls SHRINKING, b controls REMOVAL -- exactly as the notes state.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE L2 TERM LIFTS LASSO'S p > n CAP
# =====================================================================
n2, p2 = 50, 400
X2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (n2, p2))
w2 = np.zeros(p2); w2[:120] = rng.normal(0, 2, 120)     # 120 TRUE features
y2 = X2 @ w2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n2)

for tag, m in [("Lasso", Lasso(alpha=.02, max_iter=50000)),
               ("ElasticNet (r=0.5)", ElasticNet(alpha=.02, l1_ratio=.5, max_iter=50000)),
               ("ElasticNet (r=0.1)", ElasticNet(alpha=.02, l1_ratio=.1, max_iter=50000))]:
    k = int((m.fit(X2, y2).coef_ != 0).sum())
    print(f"{tag:20s} selected {k:4d} features   (n={n2}, true=120)")
# Lasso is capped at n=50. Elastic Net can exceed it.

# =====================================================================
# 7. UNIQUENESS -- the L2 term restores strict convexity
# =====================================================================
Xd = np.c_[z, z]                                        # two IDENTICAL columns
yd = 2 * z + rng.normal(0, .1, n)
print("\ntwo identical columns:")
print("  Lasso      :", Lasso(alpha=.05, max_iter=50000).fit(Xd, yd).coef_.round(4))
print("  ElasticNet :", ElasticNet(alpha=.05, l1_ratio=.5,
                                   max_iter=50000).fit(Xd, yd).coef_.round(4))
# Lasso puts everything on one (an arbitrary choice among infinitely many
# optima). Elastic Net splits it evenly -- the unique solution.

# =====================================================================
# 8. TUNING BOTH HYPERPARAMETERS
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

# ElasticNetCV uses warm starts along the path -- far cheaper than GridSearchCV
encv = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=[.1, .5, .7, .9, .95, .99, 1.0],
                 alphas=np.logspace(-4, 1, 60), cv=5,
                 max_iter=50000, random_state=0)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
best = encv[-1]
print(f"\nElasticNetCV: alpha={best.alpha_:.5f}  l1_ratio={best.l1_ratio_:.2f}")
print(f"features kept: {int((best.coef_ != 0).sum())} of {X.shape[1]}")

print(f"\n{'model':22s} {'test R2':>9s}")
for tag, m in [("OLS",        LinearRegression()),
               ("Ridge",      make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1.))),
               ("Lasso",      make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=.1, max_iter=50000))),
               ("ElasticNetCV", encv)]:
    if tag != "ElasticNetCV":
        m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{tag:22s} {m.score(X_te, y_te):9.4f}")

# The 2-D grid, if you want to see the surface:
gs = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), ElasticNet(max_iter=20000)),
                  {"elasticnet__alpha":    np.logspace(-3, 0.5, 15),
                   "elasticnet__l1_ratio": np.linspace(0.05, 1.0, 10)},
                  cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nGridSearchCV agrees:", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in gs.best_params_.items()})

# =====================================================================
# 9. FOR VERY LARGE p -- the SGD version of all three penalties
# =====================================================================
for pen, kw in [("l2", {}), ("l1", {}), ("elasticnet", {"l1_ratio": 0.5})]:
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      SGDRegressor(penalty=pen, alpha=0.01, max_iter=5000,
                                   tol=1e-6, random_state=0, **kw)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"SGD penalty={pen:12s} nonzero {int((np.abs(m[-1].coef_) > 1e-6).sum()):3d}  "
          f"test R2 {m.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
Worked Examples
Elastic Net as a blend of the two thresholds
Penalty $\lambda\big[\alpha |w| + \tfrac12 (1-\alpha) w^2\big]$ with objective $\tfrac12 (z-w)^2 + \text{penalty}$. The solution is
\hat w = \frac{S(z, \lambda\alpha)}{1+\lambda(1-\alpha)}
Set $\lambda = 1$, $z = 2.5$:

Reading it. The blend first shrinks by a constant (like Lasso) and then by a multiplicative factor (like Ridge). Lasso's zeroing can still happen when $|z|<\lambda\alpha$, while the Ridge part keeps groups of correlated features together rather than arbitrarily picking one. For correlated features this grouping is the practical reason to choose Elastic Net over Lasso.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Elastic Net is a combination of Ridge & Lasso regression. Use it
 if the dataset is large and you are confused whether to use $L_1$
 or $L_2$.

$\text{Loss}=\text{Loss}+a|w|^2+b|w|$, where
 $a$ controls shrinking the coefficients and $b$ controls
 feature removal.

It works well when the input columns have high
 multicollinearity — this is its defining advantage.

scikit-learn reparameterises to $(\alpha,\ \ell_1)$:
 alpha is the overall strength, l1_ratio is the mix.
 $b=\alpha\ell_1$ and $a=\tfrac12\alpha(1-\ell_1)$.

The constraint region morphs continuously from a circle
 ($\ell_1=0$, Ridge) to a diamond ($\ell_1=1$, Lasso).

The grouping effect: correlated predictors receive similar
 coefficients and enter or leave the model together, fixing Lasso's
 arbitrary and unstable pick among near-duplicates.

The $L_2$ term also lifts Lasso's $p>n$ selection cap and
 restores strict convexity, so the solution is unique.

Tune both hyperparameters — ElasticNetCV with warm starts is far
 cheaper than a naive grid search.

Ridge when all features matter; Lasso when most do not; Elastic Net when
 you are unsure or the features are correlated.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why does Elastic Net exist when we already have Ridge and Lasso?

Because each has a weakness the other fixes. Lasso picks arbitrarily among
correlated features and caps selection at $n$; Ridge never removes anything.
Elastic Net gets selection from the $L_1$ term and stability and grouping from the
$L_2$ term.
Q. What is the grouping effect?

With correlated predictors, the $L_2$ term forces their coefficients towards each
other — there is a bound proportional to $\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}$ on their difference
— so they enter or leave the model as a group rather than one being chosen
arbitrarily.
Q. What do alpha and l1_ratio control?

alpha is the overall regularisation strength; l1_ratio is the mix
between the two penalties. $\ell_1=0$ is pure Ridge, $\ell_1=1$ is pure Lasso.
The factorisation matters because the two are close to independent, which makes
the grid search well behaved.

Q. You have 400 features, 50 rows, and believe 120 are relevant. Which
method?

Elastic Net. Lasso is structurally capped at 50 selected features regardless of
$\alpha$; adding any $L_2$ component lifts that limit.
Q. Is Elastic Net always the safe choice?

It is the safe default when the structure is unknown, since cross-validation can
recover either extreme. The costs are a two-dimensional search and slower fitting.
When you know all features matter, or that most are noise, the single-penalty
method is simpler and equally good.
Q. Two columns are exact duplicates. What does each method do?

Lasso puts all the weight on one — an arbitrary pick among infinitely many
equally optimal solutions. Ridge splits it evenly. Elastic Net also splits it
evenly, and because the $L_2$ term makes the objective strictly convex, that
solution is provably unique.
